{{short description|Angle of complex number about real axis}}
{{distinguish|Argument of a function}}
{{other uses|Argument (disambiguation)}}
[[File:Complex_number_illustration_modarg.svg|thumb|right|Figure 1. This [[Argand diagram]] represents the [[complex number]] lying on a [[Plane (geometry)|plane]]. For each point on the plane, {{math|arg}} is the function which returns the angle <math>\varphi</math>.]]

In [[mathematics]] (particularly in [[complex analysis]]), the '''argument''' of a [[complex number]] {{mvar|z}}, denoted {{math|arg(''z'')}}, is the [[angle]] between the positive [[real number|real]] [[Cartesian coordinate system|axis]] and the line joining the origin and {{mvar|z}}, represented as a point in the [[complex plane]], shown as <math>\varphi</math> in Figure&nbsp;1. By convention the [[positive real axis]] is drawn pointing rightward, the positive [[imaginary number|imaginary]] axis is drawn pointing upward, and complex numbers with positive real part are considered to have an [[anticlockwise]] argument with positive sign.

When any real-valued angle is considered, the argument is a [[multivalued function]] operating on the nonzero complex numbers. The [[principal value]] of this function is single-valued, typically chosen to be the unique value of the argument that lies within the interval {{open-closed|−''π'', ''π''}}.<ref name=":1">{{cite web|last=Weisstein|first=Eric W.|title=Complex Argument|url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/ComplexArgument.html|access-date=2020-08-31|website=mathworld.wolfram.com|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Modulus and Argument |url=https://mas-coursebuild.ncl.ac.uk/lti/content/ASK/default/core_mathematics/pure_maths/algebra/complex_numbers/modulus_and_argument/index.html |access-date=2025-01-05 |website=mas-coursebuild.ncl.ac.uk |institution=[[Newcastle University]]}}</ref> In this article the multi-valued function will be denoted {{math|arg(''z'')}} and its principal value will be denoted {{math|Arg(''z'')}}, but in some sources the capitalization of these symbols is exchanged.

== Definition ==
[[File:Complex number illustration multiarg.svg|thumb|Figure 2. Two choices for the argument <math>\varphi</math>]]

An '''argument''' of the nonzero complex number {{math|1=''z'' = ''x'' + ''iy''}}, denoted {{math|arg(''z'')}}, is defined in two equivalent ways:
#Geometrically, in the complex plane, as the [[2D polar angle]] <math>\varphi</math> from the positive real axis to the vector representing {{mvar|z}}. The numeric value is given by the angle in [[radian]]s, and is positive if measured counterclockwise.
#Algebraically, as any real quantity <math>\varphi</math> such that
:<math display="block">z = r (\cos \varphi + i \sin \varphi) = r e^{i\varphi}</math>
for some positive real {{mvar|r}} (see [[Euler's formula]]). The quantity {{mvar|r}} is the ''[[Absolute value|modulus]]'' (or absolute value) of {{mvar|z}}, denoted {{math|{{abs|''z''}}}}:
<math display="block">r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}.</math>

The argument of zero is usually left undefined. The names ''[[magnitude (mathematics)|magnitude]],'' for the modulus, and ''[[phase (waves)|phase]]'',<ref name="phase">Dictionary of Mathematics (2002). ''phase''.</ref><ref name=":1" /> for the argument, are sometimes used equivalently.
In some older mathematical texts, the term "amplitude" was used interchangeably with argument to denote the angle of a complex number.{{efn|For example, in [[Lars Ahlfors]]' ''Complex Analysis: An introduction to the theory of analytic functions of one complex variable'' (1979), where amplitude referred to the argument of a complex number.}} While this term is largely outdated in modern texts, it still appears in some regional educational resources, where it is sometimes used in introductory-level textbooks.<ref>{{cite web |title=Modulus and Argument of a Complex Number |url=https://byjus.com/jee/complex-numbers/#modulus-and-argument-of-a-complex-number |website=Byju's |access-date=18 January 2025}}</ref>

Under both definitions, it can be seen that the argument of any non-zero complex number has many possible values: firstly, as a geometrical angle, it is clear that whole circle rotations do not change the point, so angles differing by an integer multiple of {{math|2π}} [[radian]]s (a complete [[Turn (angle)|turn]]) are the same, as reflected by figure 2 on the right. Similarly, from the [[periodic function|periodicity]] of [[sine|{{math|sin}} 
]] and [[cosine|{{math|cos}}]], the second definition also has this property.

== Principal value ==
[[File:Principal value of arg.svg|thumb|275px|Figure 3. The principal value {{math|Arg}} of the blue point at {{math|1 + ''i''}} is {{math|π/4}}. The red line here is the branch cut and corresponds to the two red lines in figure&nbsp;4 seen vertically above each other).]]

Because a complete rotation around the origin leaves a complex number unchanged, there are many choices which could be made for <math>\varphi</math> by circling the origin any number of times. This is shown in figure&nbsp;2, a representation of the [[multi-valued]] (set-valued) function <math>f(x,y)=\arg(x+iy)</math>, where a vertical line (not shown in the figure) cuts the surface at heights representing all the possible choices of angle for that point.

When a [[well-defined]] function is required, then the usual choice, known as the ''[[principal value]]'', is the value in the open-closed [[interval (mathematics)|interval]] {{open-closed|−''π'', ''π''}} radians, that is from {{math|−''π''}} to {{math|''π''}} [[radian]]s excluding {{math|−''π''}} radians itself (equiv., from −180 to +180 [[degree (angle)|degree]]s, excluding −180° itself). This represents an angle of up to half a complete circle from the positive real axis in either direction.

Some authors define the range of the principal value as being in the closed–open interval {{closed-open|0, 2''π''}}.

=== Notation ===
The principal value sometimes has the initial letter capitalized, as in {{math|Arg ''z''}}, especially when a general version of the argument is also being considered. Note that notation varies, so {{math|arg}} and {{math|Arg}} may be interchanged in different texts.

The set of all possible values of the argument can be written in terms of {{math|Arg}} as:
<math display="block">\arg(z) = \{\operatorname{Arg}(z) + 2\pi n \mid n \in \mathbb Z\}.</math>

== Computing from the real and imaginary part ==
{{main|atan2}}
If a complex number is known in terms of its real and imaginary parts, then the function that calculates the principal value {{math|Arg}} is called the [[atan2|two-argument arctangent function, {{math|atan2}}]]:
<math display="block">\operatorname{Arg}(x + iy) = \operatorname{atan2}(y,\, x)</math>
The {{math|atan2}} function is available in the math libraries of many programming languages, sometimes under a different name, and usually returns a value in the range {{open-closed|−π, π}}.<ref name=":1" />
See ''[[atan2]]'' for further detail and alternative implementations, such as
<math display="block">\operatorname{atan2}(y, x) = 2 \operatorname{atan} \frac{y}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2} + x}\,,</math>
which works except when {{tmath|1=y=0}} and {{tmath|x\le0}}, in which case the value is instead {{pi}} if {{tmath|x<0}} or undefined when {{tmath|1=x=0}}.

== Realizations of the function in computer languages ==
=== Wolfram language (Mathematica) ===
In [[Wolfram Language|Wolfram language]], there's <code>Arg[z]</code>:<ref>{{cite web|url=https://reference.wolfram.com/language/ref/Arg.html|title=Arg|work=Wolfram Language Documentation|access-date=2024-08-30}}</ref>

:<code>Arg[x + y I]</code> <math>=
\begin{cases}
  0 &\text{if } x = 0 \text{ and } y = 0, \\[5mu]
  \text{undefined} &\text{if } |x| = \infty \text{ and } |y|=\infty, \\[5mu]
  0 &\text{if } x = \infty \text{ and } |y|\ne\infty, \\[5mu]
  \pi &\text{if } x = -\infty \text{ and } |y|\ne\infty, \\[5mu]
  \pm\frac{\pi}{2} &\text{if } y = \pm\infty \text{ and } |x|\ne\infty, \\[5mu]
  \operatorname{Arg}(x + y i) &\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
</math>

or using the language's <code>ArcTan</code>:

:<code>Arg[x + y I]</code> <math>=
\begin{cases}
  0 &\text{if } x = 0 \text{ and } y = 0, \\[5mu]
  \text{ArcTan[x, y]} &\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
</math>

<code>ArcTan[x, y]</code> is <math>\operatorname{atan2}(y, x)</math> extended to work with infinities. <code>ArcTan[0, 0]</code> is <code>Indeterminate</code> (i.e. it is [[Indeterminate form|still]] defined), while <code>ArcTan[Infinity, -Infinity]</code> doesn't return anything (i.e. it is [[Undefined (mathematics)|undefined]]).

=== Maple ===
[[Maple (software)|Maple]]'s <code>argument(z)</code> behaves the same as <code>Arg[z]</code> in Wolfram language, except that <code>argument(z)</code> also returns <math>\pi</math> if <code>z</code> is the special floating-point value <code>−0.</code>.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.maplesoft.com/support/help/Maple/view.aspx?path=argument | title=Argument - Maple Help }}</ref>
Also, Maple doesn't have <math>\operatorname{atan2}</math>.

=== MATLAB ===
[[MATLAB]]'s <code>angle(z)</code> behaves<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.mathworks.com/help/matlab/ref/angle.html | title=Phase angle – MATLAB angle }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.mathworks.com/help/matlab/ref/atan2.html | title=Four-quadrant inverse tangent – MATLAB atan2 }}</ref> the same as <code>Arg[z]</code> in Wolfram language, except that it is

<math display="block">
\begin{cases}
  \frac{1\pi}{4} &\text{if } x = \infty \text{ and } y = \infty, \\[5mu]
  -\frac{1\pi}{4} &\text{if } x = \infty \text{ and } y = -\infty, \\[5mu]
  \frac{3\pi}{4} &\text{if } x = -\infty \text{ and } y = \infty, \\[5mu]
  -\frac{3\pi}{4} &\text{if } x = -\infty \text{ and } y = -\infty.
\end{cases}
</math>

Unlike in Maple and Wolfram language, MATLAB's <code>atan2(y, x)</code> is equivalent to <code>angle(x + y*1i)</code>. That is, <code>atan2(0, 0)</code> is <math>0</math>.

== Identities ==
One of the main motivations for defining the principal value {{math|Arg}} is to be able to write complex numbers in modulus-argument form. Hence for any complex number {{mvar|z}},
<math display="block">z = \left| z \right| e^{i \operatorname{Arg} z}.</math>

This is only really valid if {{mvar|z}} is non-zero, but can be considered valid for {{math|1=''z'' = 0}} if <math>\operatorname{Arg}0</math> is considered as an [[indeterminate form]]—rather than as being undefined.

Some further identities follow. If {{math|''z''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|''z''<sub>2</sub>}} are two non-zero complex numbers, then
<math display="block">\begin{align}
                    \operatorname{Arg}(z_1  z_2) &\equiv \operatorname{Arg}z_1 + \operatorname{Arg}z_2 \pmod{\left(-\pi,\pi\right]}, \\
  \operatorname{Arg}\frac{z_1}{z_2} &\equiv \operatorname{Arg}z_1 - \operatorname{Arg}z_2 \pmod{\left(-\pi,\pi\right]},
\end{align}</math>
where <math>(\operatorname{mod}\left(-\pi,\pi\right])</math> means to add or subtract any integer multiple of {{math|2''&pi;''}} if necessary to bring the value into the interval of {{open-closed|−''π'', ''π''}} radians. In particular,
<math display="block">\operatorname{Arg}(-z) \equiv \operatorname{Arg}z+\pi\begin{cases}1,&\operatorname{Im}z<0,\\\operatorname{sgn}z,&\operatorname{Im}z=0,\\-1,&\operatorname{Im}z>0.\\\end{cases}</math>

If {{math|''z'' ≠ 0}} and {{mvar|n}} is any integer, then<ref name=":1" />
<math display="block">\operatorname{Arg}\left(z^n\right) \equiv n \operatorname{Arg}z \pmod{\left(-\pi,\pi\right]}.</math>

=== Example ===
<math display="block">\operatorname{Arg}\left(\frac{-1- i}i\right) = \left(\operatorname{Arg}(-1 - i) - \operatorname{Arg}i = -\frac{3\pi}4 - \frac\pi2 = -\frac{5\pi}4\right)\pmod{\left(-\pi,\pi\right]}=\frac{3\pi}4.</math>

=== Using the complex logarithm ===

From <math>z = |z| e^{i \operatorname{Arg}z}</math>, we get <math>i \operatorname{Arg}z = \ln \frac{z}{|z|}</math>, alternatively <math>\operatorname{Arg}(z) = \operatorname{Im}\ln \frac{z}{|z|} =  \operatorname{Im}\ln z</math>. As we are taking the imaginary part, any normalization by a real scalar will not affect the result. This is useful when one has the [[complex logarithm]] available.

=== Differentiation ===

The argument function is not complex differentiable, as the limit
<math display="block">\lim\limits_{z\to z_0}\frac{\arg z-\arg z_0}{z-z_0}</math>
does not exist for any <math>z_0\in\mathbb{C}</math> and on any branch (indeed, for any chosen branch the numerator takes the same value). However, the [[Wirtinger derivatives]] may be applied to it. Begin from the logarithmic identity
<math display="block">\ln z=\operatorname{Ln}|z|+i\arg z.</math>
Use that <math>|z|^{2}=z\bar{z}</math>:
<math display="block">\ln z=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Ln} z +\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Ln}\bar{z}+i\arg z.</math>
Performing different branch cuts lets one apply the derivatives to all points of the principal logarithm in two goes. First, apply <math>\frac{\partial}{\partial z}</math>:
<math display="block">\frac{1}{z}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{z}+0+i\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\arg z.</math>
Rearranging gives <math>\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\arg z=\frac{-i}{2z}</math>. Now apply <math>\frac{\partial}{\partial\bar{z}}</math>:
<math display="block">0=0+\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{\bar{z}}+i\frac{\partial}{\partial\bar{z}}\arg z.</math>
This shows that <math>\frac{\partial}{\partial\bar{z}}\arg z=\frac{i}{2\bar{z}}</math>.
As both Wirtinger derivatives exist, one can then apply the Dolbeault derivatives,
<math display="block">\partial\arg(z)=\frac{-i}{2z}\,dz,</math>
<math display="block">\bar{\partial}\arg(z)=\frac{i}{2\bar{z}}\,d\bar{z}.</math>
This then means the [[exterior derivative]] exists, given by their sum,
<math display="block">d\arg(z)=\frac{-i}{2z}\,dz+\frac{i}{2\bar{z}}\,d\bar{z}.</math>
This is an important [[differential form]], as it is precisely the generator of the first [[de Rham cohomology]] of the circle, <math>H^{1}_{dR}(S^{1})</math>. In other words,
<math display="block">d\arg(z)=\frac{-i}{2z}\,dz+\frac{i}{2\bar{z}}\,d\bar{z}=\frac{x\,dy-y\,dx}{x^{2}+y^{2}},</math>
making this form closed but not exact in the usual sense (a byproduct of being multivalued):
<math display="block">\oint\limits_{S^1}d\arg(z)=2\pi>0</math>
with the standard orientation.
